newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: OLYMPICS-ATLANTA PROBLEMS STILL VERY MUCH ON OLYMPIC MINDS.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-ATLANTA PROBLEMS STILL VERY MUCH ON OLYMPIC MINDS.

text.p: Organisers of the next Olympics in Japan admitted on Thursday that they were under extra pressure to run a trouble-free event after the calamitous organisation at this year's Atlanta Games.

Officials from Nagano, which hosts the Winter Games in 1998, were warned by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) to avoid the accreditation, transport and computer problems which made life difficult for athletes, officials and the media in Atlanta.
Asked if there was more pressure after the Summer Games' problems, Nagano director Makoto Kobayashi said: "Yes, especially regarding transport and information."

In Atlanta, competitors, officials and the media were often forced to wait for hours at the airport to get their identification cards and were frustrated by the inefficient bus system taking them to venues.
The computer system for results also failed to work at the start of the Games which was criticised by the media worldwide.

Nagano chiefs have already held talks with the multi- national computer firm IBM about the technological problems and are working to make sure athletes should not be forced to wait around for a long time for accreditation after long flights to Japan.
Atlanta was also heavily criticised for commercial excesses. Some said the large number of city-backed private vendors allowed to clog the city centre had made the Games look like a huge flea market.
Ironically the subject was not discussed when Japanese officials met the IOC executive board on Wednesday.
But Kobayashi said: "There is no way the city will set up such commercial ventures."

The IOC has yet to carry out its full post-mortem on Atlanta although general director Francois Carrard said after the board meeting that there were already proposals to revamp the accreditation procedure to avoid huge queues.

Salt Lake City, the U.S. hosts of the 2002 Winter Olympics, came under fire from the IOC on Wednesday for being slow to clinch a marketing deal -- the all-important corporate sponsorships which help fund the Games.
Vice-president Dick Pound said things were moving at "glacial speed."

But the IOC's tone changed dramatically on Thursday when organisers were able to tell the executive board that they had struck a deal with national Olympic officials about sponsors and planned to have a contract drawn up by the end of the year.
